title: Missing the Wood for the Trees
author: David Didau
summary: Two studies claiming that domain-adjacent prior knowledge fails to support learning rest on a methodological mistake: they assume any increase in knowledge should produce gains on any chosen assessment, ignoring whether the assessment actually depends on the knowledge taught. Buchin and Mulligan taught acoustic, tactile, and chemical perception but tested color perception, which depends on foundational science schema most teens already hold. The Education Endowment Foundation's Word and World trial taught history and geography but measured progress on decoding and inference, which the content does not address. When the conceptual bridge between content and assessment is missing, null effects are guaranteed. Prior knowledge supports learning only when ideas genuinely interlock structurally, not when they are thematically adjacent.
points: Studies reporting that prior domain knowledge fails to boost new learning usually rest on methodological error: they test whether taught content helps with assessments that don't depend on it.
The conceptual bridge matters more than the label: color perception requires foundational science schema; teaching more chemistry won't help.
Prior knowledge supports learning only when ideas genuinely interlock structurally, not when they are thematically adjacent.
Teachers often conflate proximity with prerequisite: if a student can't infer, giving more historical facts won't help because the problem isn't domain knowledge, it's the thinking skill.
The maxim that prior knowledge is the most important factor in learning remains true, provided that knowledge belongs to the structure of the new idea, not merely to its theme.
quotes: The claim that domain-adjacent prior knowledge does not support new in-domain learning looks, at first glance, like a body-blow to one of the most widely quoted maxims in educational psychology. If “the most important factor in learning is what students already know,” how can a new experimental study report that supplying domain-related knowledge makes no difference at all?

If this looks uncannily like the result reported by Buchin and Mulligan, that’s because both studies hinge on the same conceptual mistake. They assume that any increase in knowledge should automatically produce gains on any chosen assessment.

In both studies the same problem recurs: students were assessed on tasks that did not depend on the knowledge they had been taught. When the conceptual bridge between content and assessment is missing, null effects are almost guaranteed.

Predictive processing does not explain the failure of either study so much as re-describe it in more elaborate terms. The moment we abandon the assumption that the researchers actually supplied the prior knowledge the target task depended on, the puzzle evaporates. The flaw is methodological, not metaphysical.
Prior knowledge supports learning only when ideas genuinely interlock. It is the structure of the content, not the thematic label, that determines what counts as a prerequisite.

If a child cannot ride a bike because they cannot balance, no one suggests giving them a rocking horse and hoping the skill will emerge. And yet, when we step into academic domains, the clarity sometimes evaporates. A student who struggles to infer meaning from a passage in history is often given yet more historical facts, as if additional detail about the Battle of Hastings will compensate for not understanding how inference works.

We get distracted by domain labels and thematic proximity; we assume that because ideas sit near each other conceptually, one must support the other. Without the intuitive scaffolding of everyday contexts, we lose our grip on what is prerequisite and what is merely adjacent.

The most important factor in learning remains what students already know, provided that what they already know belongs to the structure of the new idea. Everything else, however close it might appear, is wood mistaken for trees.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
